<p class="eyebrow">Research</p>
<h1>Imaging hidden environments.</h1>
<p class="lead">I use seismic observations to investigate subsurface structure across continental and polar environments. A central question is how these observations can help us infer material composition, porosity, and physical state—and how confidently we can make those inferences.</p>

<section id="antarctica" class="research-story">
<div class="wrap">
<p class="number">01 / ANTARCTIC SUBGLACIAL GEOPHYSICS</p>
<div class="story-grid">
<div>
<h2>Beneath the Antarctic Ice Sheet</h2>
<p class="question">What can geophysical observations tell us about the physical and hydrological state of the subglacial environment? </p>
<p>My current research focuses on understanding what lies beneath the Antarctic Ice Sheet and how subglacial conditions influence the ice above. I use dense seismic observations, together with complementary radar and magnetotelluric constraints, to characterize subglacial sediments, hydrology, and basal conditions.</p>
<p>Building on this work, I aim to develop integrated seismic–radar approaches for imaging and characterizing the sub-ice environment, with the broader goal of understanding how subglacial properties and hydrological processes shape ice–bed interactions.</p>
</div>

<section id="continental" class="research-story">
<div class="wrap">
<p class="number">02 / CONTINENTAL SEISMIC IMAGING &amp; JOINT INVERSION</p>
<div class="story-grid">
<div>
<h2>More information.<br>Better constraints.</h2>
<p class="question">How can multiple seismic observables reduce ambiguity in crustal imaging?</p>
<p>I develop joint-inversion methods that combine complementary seismic observations to constrain crustal structure and reduce parameter trade-offs. A substantial part of my doctoral work applies these approaches to large-scale USArray datasets to investigate spatial variations across the continental United States. This work also motivates my broader interest in connecting seismic structure to the composition and physical state of subsurface materials.</p>
<a class="text-link" href="https://doi.org/10.1029/2023JB027952">Read the 2024 JGR paper</a>
</div>

<li>Rayleigh-wave H/V and amplification</li>
<li>Monte Carlo joint inversion</li>
</ul>

<section id="computational" class="research-story">
<div class="wrap">
<p class="number">03 / COMPUTATIONAL GEOPHYSICS &amp; UNCERTAINTY</p>
<div class="story-grid">
<div>
<h2>Beyond a single best-fitting model.</h2>
<p class="question">Which features are well constrained—and where does uncertainty remain?</p>
<p>Geophysical imaging requires both efficient computation and a clear understanding of model uncertainty. My computational work spans Monte Carlo and Bayesian inversion, large-scale seismic data processing, and HPC/GPU workflows.</p>
<p>During a research internship at TGS in summer 2026, I developed and productionized Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) workflows for uncertainty quantification in 3-D/4-D acoustic full-waveform inversion.</p>
</div>
